newsitem.title: USA: Dow soars as rate fears calm, Nasdaq scores record.
newsitem.headline: Dow soars as rate fears calm, Nasdaq scores record.

text.p: U.S. stocks wiped out Friday's losses, led by a tech sector rally, as investors took a weekend break and concluded Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan would not be raising interest rates in the near future.

"The underlying fundamental is (that) Greenspan is not in a position to raise rates," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney. "We had a sigh of relief after enough action on Friday" when the Dow industrials fell some 140 points intraday before ending down 56 points.
The Dow ended up 82 points to about 6464.
It was the blue chip index's biggest point gain since November 6's 97-point gain in a post-election euphoria.
The tech-studded Nasdaq Composite surged 29 points to an unofficial record close of 1316, topping December 3's 1300.37.
Winners beat losers 19-6 on active NYSE volume of about 380 million shares.

Friday's sell-off was sparked by Greenspan's comments late Thursday to the American Enterprise Institute that "irrational" market exuberance could damage the economy. Investors initially saw his remarks as meaning Greenspan stood ready to raise rates if the stock market was overheating, analysts and traders said.
But investors reassessed the comments over the weekend and the long bond surged 19/32 to yield 6.47 percent. The yield on Friday had risen to 6.54 percent -- the highest in a month.

"I think Greenspan is saying he wants us to be cautious, not comfortable about where the market is right now. Cautious does not mean bearish," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.

"What we're seeing in the Dow and S&P 500 is a continuation of the snapback we saw Friday (off session lows). Don't expect this to start a run on these stocks. We've just gotten back what we lost Friday." The S&P 500 rose 10 to 750.

Cripps added, "Last week, we started to see signs of a trend toward secondary stocks and non-S&P 500s -- it's very evident here. Small and mid-caps are outperforming today ... as portfolio managers find better ideas and better names away from the top 50 names." The Russell 2000 index of smaller company stocks rallied five points or 1.40 percent to 360.

Nonetheless, large cap high-techs lured strong buying. IBM surged 4-3/8 to 160 and Microsoft jumped 5-3/8 to 81-3/4 in its first day of trading after a two-for-one stock split. Intel climbed 4-7/16 to 130-1/8 and Cypress Semiconductor added 1-5/8 to 15-1/2.
Compaq Computer rose two to 85-3/4. Merrill Lynch raised 1996 and 1997 earnings estimates.
Among individual stocks, Dow component Philip Morris rallied 4-3/4 to 114-1/4, giving the Dow a 15 point boost. Goldman raised its 12-month price target to $135 from $125.

Santa Fe Pacific Gold rose 1-1/4 to 16-1/2 after Homestake Mining emerged as a white knight bidder with a buyout offer of $17.42 a share or $2.3 billion. The offer follows Newmont Mining's proposal last Thursday to buy Santa Fe for $2 billion in stock. Homestake fell 7/8 to 14-3/4 and Newmont Mining rose 1/8 to 47

Centennial Technologies rallied five to 46-1/4. It acquired a 12 percent interest in ViA Inc for undisclosed terms. ViA is a privately held technology company that actively designs, develops and markets miniature communication and computing products.
British Airways rose 3-7/8 to 99-1/4 in U.S. trading amid signs Britain would approve an alliance with AMR Corp's American Airlines. AMR added 2-1/4 to 91-3/4.
UroQuest Medical rose 1-3/4 to 7-1/2. Prudential Securities started coverage of the stock with a buy rating.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 28.59 to 1316.27, a record.
The S&P 500 rose 10.16 to 749.76.
(Figures official as of 1645 EST/2145 GMT).
-- Wall Street Desk 212-859-1721
